questions.q: Which of these problems is the best fit for a frequency counter?
questions.explain: "Same items, any order" depends only on how often each code appears, which is exactly what a frequency table keeps. Runs and consecutive windows depend on positions, and a sorted search depends on order: those need other patterns.
options: Find the longest run of consecutive on-time deliveries
Decide whether two packing lists contain the same item codes, in any order
Find the position of order ORD-77 in a list sorted by id
Find the maximum revenue over any 7 consecutive days

questions.q: A frequency table of a string keeps each character's count. What information does it throw away?
questions.explain: The table is a summary without positions. That is why it answers "same letters?" in O(n), and why it cannot answer order-dependent questions such as "is a ever followed by b?". (The total length can still be recovered by adding up the counts.)
options: How many characters there are in total
Nothing; the string can be rebuilt from the table

questions.q: The "find and cross off" anagram check searches the remaining letters of b for each letter of a. With both strings of length n, how does its work grow?
questions.explain: Each of the n searches can scan up to n letters, about n(n + 1) / 2 comparisons in the worst case, and splice adds more shifting on top. Ten times longer input means about a hundred times more work.

questions.q: Why does this module compare solutions by counting operations instead of timing them?
questions.explain: Timings vary between runs and machines. Counting the operation in the innermost loop gives a number that is reproducible and shows the growth rate directly.
options: Timers are not available in Node.js
A count depends only on the algorithm and the input, while a time also depends on the machine, other programs, the JIT and the garbage collector
Counting is always faster than timing
Operation counts are always equal to milliseconds

questions.q: A developer checks anagrams by testing that the strings have the same length and that new Set(a) and new Set(b) hold the same characters. Which pair does it get wrong?
questions.explain: A Set keeps which values appear, not how many times. "aab" and "abb" have the same set {a, b} (and even the same length) but different counts, so they are not anagrams. Counts are the whole point.

questions.q: What goes wrong if you write counts.set(x, counts.get(x) + 1) instead of using ?? 0?
questions.explain: A missing key reads as undefined. ?? 0 turns "not seen yet" into a count of 0. Once a count is NaN, adding to it keeps it NaN.
options: The first time a value is seen, counts.get(x) is undefined, and undefined + 1 is NaN, so every count becomes NaN

questions.q: sameItems counts up for every item of a and down for every item of b. When does it return false during the second loop?
questions.explain: A count of 0 means every copy a had has already been matched. The final check (open === 0) catches the opposite case, where a has items left over.
options: When an item of b has a count greater than 1
When an item of b has a count of 0: b has an item a does not, or one copy too many
When the two items at the same index differ
Never; it only decides at the end

questions.q: sameItems ends with return open === 0. If you replaced that line with return true, which call would give a wrong answer?
questions.explain: The second loop only fails when b asks for something a has run out of, so it catches "ab"/"abb" and "aab"/"abb" by itself. When a is the longer one, every item of b finds a match and the loop finishes; only the leftover open count (one b never matched) shows that a had more. Two empty strings really are anagrams.

questions.q: To find the first transfer reference that appears only once in a log, why does the solution walk the log twice?
questions.explain: During the first pass you cannot know yet whether a reference will appear again later. Two O(n) passes are still O(n). (Iterating the Map in insertion order would also work here, but walking the input states the intent directly.)
options: The first pass builds the counts; the table has no positions, so a second pass over the log in order finds the earliest reference with count 1
Because a Map can only be read once
It does not need to; the first key in the Map is always the answer

questions.q: Why can a list have at most one majority element (a value appearing more than n / 2 times)?
questions.explain: "More than half" is strict. Two values with exactly half each is a tie, and neither is a majority.
options: Because Maps cannot store two majorities
Two such values would need more than n / 2 + n / 2 = n items between them, more than the list holds
It can have two if they tie

questions.q: Why does the Boyer–Moore majority vote need a second, verifying pass?
questions.explain: When a majority exists, the vote always ends with it. When none exists, the vote still ends with some candidate. Only counting tells the two cases apart.
options: Because the first pass may miss the true majority
If there is no majority, the surviving candidate is just a leftover value, so you must count it to confirm it really appears more than n / 2 times
It does not; the candidate is always the majority

questions.q: Boyer–Moore uses O(1) space; a frequency table uses O(k). Why is the frequency table still called "the pattern"?
questions.explain: Specialised tricks trade generality for resources. Start with the general pattern and reach for the trick only when memory really matters.
options: The table answers any counting question (majority, first unique, top method, containment); the vote solves only the majority problem
Because O(1) space is impossible in JavaScript

questions.q: When is an array of counters a better frequency table than a Map?
questions.explain: With a fixed alphabet the array has a constant size, no hashing and no hash worst case, and joining it gives a signature string. For open-ended values such as ids, a Map is the right table.
options: When the values are order ids
When the values come from a small alphabet known in advance, such as a–z and 0–9, so each value maps directly to an index
When the values can be any string

questions.q: Two usernames get the signature counts.join(",") from a 36-slot counter array. When are their signatures equal?
questions.explain: Equal signatures mean equal counts for every character, which is the definition of an anagram. That is why a Map from signature to names finds impersonators with one lookup.
options: When they have the same length
When they start with the same letter
Exactly when they are anagrams (after normalisation)
Only when they are the same username

questions.q: There are 200,000 protected usernames. Why build a signature index instead of calling sameItems against each on every sign-up?
questions.explain: Precomputing an index is the lookup pattern from Hash maps and sets, applied to a key you compute from counts. The price is memory for the index and keeping it up to date.
options: Because sameItems gives wrong answers for long lists
The index does the counting work once; each sign-up then costs one signature (O(L)) and one Map lookup, instead of 200,000 comparisons
Because Maps use less memory than arrays

questions.q: The signature function throws on a character outside the alphabet instead of skipping it. Why?
questions.explain: A counter that ignores unknown characters changes the question it answers. Decide the valid alphabet at the boundary and refuse anything else loudly.
options: Skipping would silently make bola-support look like an anagram of bolasupport; rejecting unexpected input is safer than guessing what it means
So that the index stays sorted

questions.q: You count 1,000,000 order ids and every id is different. How big is the frequency table?
questions.explain: The extra space is O(k), where k is the number of distinct values. For unique ids k = n. For letters, k is small however long the text is.
options: O(n): one entry per distinct id, so a million entries

questions.q: A customer's name is stored as "josé" in one system and "josé" in another. Both print as josé. What should a counter do before counting?
questions.explain: Unicode allows the same visible text in composed and decomposed forms. Without normalisation they are different strings and different keys, so counts and anagram checks disagree.
options: Normalise both with .normalize("NFC"), so the accented letter has one form

questions.q: Why is a Map safer than a plain object for counting values that come from users?
questions.explain: A Map has no inherited keys and stores any key literally. (It does not normalise anything: "Ada" and "ada" are still different keys.)
options: Plain objects have inherited keys such as constructor, and "__proto__" never becomes a normal key, so some values are counted wrongly

questions.q: Which question can a single frequency table NOT answer?
questions.explain: "Within 10 minutes" depends on positions in time, which a whole-list table has thrown away. A sliding window, which counts only the items inside a moving range, fits that question.
options: Does any payment reference appear twice?
Which delivery zone appears most often?
Did the same reference appear twice within 10 minutes?
Can this order be fulfilled from this stock list?

questions.q: The transfers live in PostgreSQL. What is the best way to find references that appear exactly once?
questions.explain: It is the same pattern, run next to the data, so millions of rows never travel over the network. The database builds its own counting table or sorts internally.
options: Load all rows into Node.js and use nested loops
Load all rows into Node.js and use a Map
Let the database count: GROUP BY ref HAVING COUNT(*) = 1
Sort the rows in the browser

questions.q: The test compares sameItems with a sort-based version on 5,000 random word pairs, and prints how many pairs were anagrams. Why print that number?
questions.explain: A random test is only as good as the cases it happens to generate. Using a three-letter alphabet makes anagrams common, and the printed count shows it.
options: To prove the random inputs exercised both outcomes; if no pair was ever an anagram, "5000/5000 agree" would say little about the true case
Because the sort-based version is wrong
To measure how fast the test ran

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A Map keeps insertion order: b, then a, then n. Each entry is a [key, count] array, and joining an array of arrays with a space turns each inner array into "key,count".

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The first Yaba computes undefined + 1, which is NaN, and NaN + 1 stays NaN. Ikeja was never set, so it reads as undefined.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: "aab"/"abb" fails when the second b finds a count of 0. "ab"/"abb" fails the same way. "abb"/"ab" matches every item of b, but one b is left open, so the final check returns false.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: In SAVE2SAVE every letter appears twice and only 2 appears once. In NGN, N appears twice, so G is first. AABB has no unique character.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Two As out of four is exactly half, not more than half. Two Bs out of three is more than 1.5. A single item is always the majority of a one-item list.

questions.q: What does this print? (The vote without the verifying pass.)
questions.explain: In the first list Yaba and Lekki cancel, then Ikeja becomes the candidate, although it appears only once. That is why the real function verifies the candidate with a second pass. In the second list Lekki is a true majority and survives.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: The emoji is one code point stored as two UTF-16 code units. length and split("") count code units; spread and for...of iterate code points.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: On a plain object, counts["__proto__"] reads the prototype (an object, not undefined), so the sum is the string "[object Object]1", and assigning a value that is not an object to __proto__ is ignored. The count never appears as a key. A Map would count it normally.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Stock has two OIL and one RICE. The order uses both OIL units and the RICE; the third OIL finds a count of 0 and is missing.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Slot 0 counts a, slot 1 b, slot 2 c. The empty word still produces three zero counters, so its signature is 0,0,0, not an empty string.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Without normalisation all four strings are different keys. After trimming and upper-casing, there are two ids, each appearing twice: two duplicates the raw count would have missed.

questions.q: Write isAnagram(a, b) for usernames with a frequency counter (no sorting). Lower-case both first and ignore _ and .. Print the three results on one line.
questions.explain: Count up for a, down for b, fail on a count of 0, and require nothing left open at the end. "aab"/"abb" tests the counts; "kemi"/"mikee" tests unequal lengths.

questions.q: Every transfer reference should appear twice in the log (debit and credit). Print the first reference, in log order, that appears only once, or null. Use O(n) time.
questions.explain: Pass one counts; pass two walks the log in order and stops at the first count of 1. Two linear passes are O(n) time, with O(k) space for the table.

questions.q: Implement the Boyer–Moore majority vote with a verifying pass. Print the majority zone of each list, or null.
questions.explain: Without the verifying pass, the second list would return Ikeja, the last survivor, which appears only once. O(n) time and O(1) space.

questions.q: Print true if the order can be packed from the stock (every unit of the order is available, counts included), otherwise false. Use a frequency table of the stock.
questions.explain: This is the anagram check without the final "nothing left over" test: stock may hold extra items. O(s + o) time, O(k) space for the stock table.

questions.q: Print the payment methods used most often, as an array, keeping ties. Use one counting pass and one pass over the table.
questions.explain: A strict > starts a new list; an equal count joins it. Map iteration order (first appearance) decides the order of tied methods.

questions.q: An imported list of usernames must not contain two names that are equal after trimming and lower-casing. Print each duplicated (normalised) username once, in the order its second copy appears.
questions.explain: Reporting at the moment a count reaches exactly 2 gives each duplicate once, in the order it was discovered; a third copy (count 3) is not reported again.

questions.q: Group the usernames that are anagrams of each other and print only the groups with more than one name. Build each key by sorting the characters of the lower-cased name (sorting a short name is fine here).
questions.explain: Any key that is equal exactly for anagrams works: sorted characters, or a counts signature. The Map groups names by that key in one pass; tunde is alone in its group and is filtered out.

questions.q: Count the comparisons the nested-loop duplicate check makes on 1,000 distinct order ids (compare every pair once, j starting at i + 1), and the number of Map updates a frequency counter makes on the same list. Print both numbers.
questions.explain: The nested loops compare every pair once: n(n − 1) / 2 = 499,500. The counter touches each id once: 1,000. That ratio, n/2, keeps growing with n.
